labels.definition: Information, research, treatments or people are described as censored, suppressed, buried or silenced. "They never talk about X" with no question is this frame, not `frame:insinuating_questions`.
labels.name: Censorship & suppression framing

labels.definition: A coordinated, hidden and malign effort is alleged. Requires an actual allegation of coordination or concealment; criticism, distrust, incompetence, concealment by one named person or firm without coordination, or documented misconduct narrated as fact is not enough.
labels.name: Conspiracy / cover-up

concepts: why won't they test that? coincidence?
labels.definition: A suspicion is advanced through leading questions or "makes you wonder" insinuation rather than asserted. Requires a question or a "makes you wonder" phrase.
labels.name: Insinuating questions ("just asking")

labels.definition: Health threats are presented in alarmist, catastrophic language meant to provoke alarm. Needs intensification beyond the standard term: "obesity epidemic", "opioid crisis" or "loneliness epidemic" used descriptively is not it.
labels.name: Fear & crisis framing

labels.definition: Health decisions are framed as autonomy, informed consent, parental rights or freedom from mandates.
labels.name: Medical-freedom framing

labels.definition: Ordinary judgement, lived experience or independent research is elevated over expertise and credentials.
labels.name: Anti-expert / populist framing

labels.definition: Something is recommended or condemned because it is natural, ancestral, traditional, evolutionary, artificial or synthetic, including design language without God or spirit. "Toxic", "clean", "chemicals" and "poison" are `frame:toxin_purity`.
labels.name: Naturalness & ancestral appeal

labels.definition: Health problems are framed in terms of toxins, poisons, chemical burden or clean-versus-contaminated bodies and products. Not for "eat clean" as an idiom for healthy eating.
labels.name: Toxin & purity framing

labels.definition: Health is framed as performance to maximize through protocols, stacks, metrics and hacks. Needs maximizing language applied to the body; everyday "optimal" and lab ranges are not it.
labels.name: Optimization & biohacking framing

labels.definition: The Make America Healthy Again framing. Needs at least two of: a chronic-disease crisis, especially in children; causes in food, chemicals or medicine; corporate or government capture; the movement or its agenda named. The slogan or one concern alone is not it.
labels.name: MAHA framing

labels.definition: A health issue is framed through partisan or culture-war identity: a party or a culture-war camp ("the left", "woke medicine", "gender ideology activists") is blamed or praised as a political camp, even when no party is named.
labels.name: Partisan framing

labels.definition: Health is framed in religious or spiritual terms: divine design, sin, faith, prayer or spiritual causes of illness. Design language without God or spirit is `frame:naturalness_appeal`.
labels.name: Spiritual & religious framing

labels.definition: The passage sells or monetizes: sponsorship, discount codes, affiliate links, or the speaker's own product, clinic, programme or book. Apply to a host's own products as well as paid reads.
labels.name: Commercialization

labels.definition: The speaker disclaims medical authority or responsibility, or advises consulting a professional.
labels.name: Disclaimer

labels.definition: The speaker corrects, fact-checks or debunks a health claim, whether or not the correction is itself accurate.
labels.name: Correction & debunking

labels.definition: An identifiable study is invoked: a finding plus at least one of a named author or research group, journal, institution, or trial or dataset name, or a year together with a design. A design, sample size or year alone with a finding is `evidence:vague_research`.
labels.name: Specific study citation

labels.definition: Research or experts are invoked without enough to identify a study: "studies show", a study given only by design, size or year, a named scientist's theory or body of work, or unnamed experts. Agreement among experts is `evidence:expert_consensus`; a media source is `evidence:media_source`.
labels.name: Vague research appeal

labels.definition: Government or official data, records, documents or findings are invoked as evidence: numbers, databases, regulated labels (drug label, package insert), filings, and an official body's assessment or finding. An official recommendation or advisory is `evidence:expert_consensus`.
labels.name: Official data & documents

labels.definition: Expert agreement, a guideline, an official recommendation or advisory, or a classification decision is invoked as support, including a journal named as a guideline's source. Unnamed experts without asserted agreement are `evidence:vague_research`.
labels.name: Consensus, guideline & official-recommendation appeal

labels.definition: A prestigious institution, journal or award is named to lend authority rather than a finding discussed on its content.
labels.name: Prestige-institution invocation

labels.definition: A named person's title, training or professional identity is invoked as grounds for believing a claim, including their recommendation given with their title. Anonymous endorsements are `evidence:strength_assertion`.
labels.name: Credential appeal

concepts: we see this all the time in clinic
labels.definition: A practitioner's own experience treating, coaching or advising people about their health, licensed or not (doctors, therapists, dietitians, chiropractors, naturopaths, health coaches, trainers). Treat the speaker as a practitioner only if the window says so; another practitioner's results or a relayed patient story is `evidence:personal_anecdote`.
labels.name: Clinical experience

labels.definition: Personal or second-hand experience is offered as grounds for a general conclusion, including relayed patient stories and non-health professional or eyewitness experience.
labels.name: Personal anecdote & testimonial

labels.definition: A biological mechanism is used to explain a claim or make it plausible. It can co-occur with study signals.
labels.name: Mechanistic explanation

labels.definition: An explicit assertion about the evidence or proof behind something (proven, science-backed, FDA approved offered as grounds), an anonymous endorsement or certification seal, or "there's no evidence" used as a verdict. Certainty boosters alone ("we know", "clearly") are not this label.
labels.name: Evidence-strength assertion

labels.definition: Animal, cell or lab evidence is offered as support for a claim about humans.
labels.name: Preclinical extrapolation

labels.definition: Preliminary, observational or single-case human evidence is offered: association, small pilot, case report, preprint, survey, or unattributed statistics or survey figures. Code the kind offered, not your opinion of a plain citation.
labels.name: Preliminary or observational human evidence

labels.definition: Long or traditional use is offered as evidence.
labels.name: Traditional-use appeal

labels.definition: Other countries' rules, practices or outcomes are offered as evidence.
labels.name: Foreign-comparison appeal

labels.definition: A media source, named or not, is offered as where the speaker learned something: a book, documentary, news report, video, podcast or podcast guest's statement, quote, social-media post, historical document, biography, or private email or letter. "Research" or "studies" as the source is `evidence:vague_research`.
labels.name: Media or social source

labels.definition: The speaker acknowledges limits or uncertainty in the evidence, including saying evidence is absent when acknowledging uncertainty rather than giving a verdict.
labels.name: Evidence limitations acknowledged

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about babies or toddlers (under about 3): "babies", "toddlers", "under 3".
labels.name: Infants & toddlers

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about school-age children or "kids" generally: "kids", "children", "school-age", "young girls", and "minors" unless ages 13 to 17 are given.
labels.name: Children

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about teenagers or adolescents: "teens", "adolescents", ages 13 to 17.
labels.name: Adolescents & teens

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about young adults (roughly 18 to 30), including "Gen Z" and "young people" when adults are meant.
labels.name: Young adults

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about pregnant or postpartum people. Pregnancy or postpartum content takes this label only, not `population:women`.
labels.name: Pregnant & postpartum people

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about women's health as women.
labels.name: Women

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about men's health as men.
labels.name: Men

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about people in midlife (roughly 40 to 64).
labels.name: Midlife adults

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about older adults: 65+ or described as elderly, seniors or ageing parents.
labels.name: Older adults

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about LGBTQ or transgender people.
labels.name: LGBTQ people

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about athletes or the highly active.
labels.name: Athletes & highly active people

labels.definition: The health content is specifically about service members or veterans.
labels.name: Military & veterans
